venues.name: Four Seasons Hotel Mexico City
venues.note: A hacienda-style house wrapped around a green courtyard on Reforma, the city's most complete grand-hotel service, and a calm oasis off the boulevard.

venues.name: The St. Regis Mexico City
venues.note: A César Pelli tower over Reforma with the Angel of Independence at its feet, St. Regis butler service and one of the best skyline views in the capital.

venues.name: Las Alcobas, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.note: A jewel-box on Polanco's luxury-shopping avenue, 35 rooms of quiet, warm-toned design, steps from the boutiques and the great tables.

venues.name: Casa Polanco
venues.note: Two 1940s mansions woven into one 19-room house facing Lincoln Park, the only Two-Key hotel in the city, and its most refined address.
credentials: MICHELIN Two Keys (2025), the only Two-Key hotel in Mexico City

venues.name: Sofitel Mexico City Reforma
venues.note: A sleek French-accented tower on Reforma, crowned by the 38th-floor Cityzen rooftop, grand views and a lively social scene under one roof.

venues.name: Pug Seal Allan Poe
venues.note: A colour-drenched, art-filled boutique house on a quiet Polanco street, bold design, 24-hour pantry and a temazcal ritual on site.

venues.name: Brick Hotel Mexico City
venues.note: An early-20th-century mansion turned intimate hotel in the heart of Roma Norte, Belle Époque bones, a courtyard and a good restaurant.

venues.name: La Valise Mexico City
venues.note: A three-suite townhouse of theatrical, one-of-a-kind rooms, a bed that rolls onto the balcony is the signature, pure Roma romance.

venues.name: Octavia Casa
venues.note: A serene, minimalist house by fashion designer Roberta Maceda in leafy Condesa, natural materials, calm light and quiet good taste.

venues.name: Ignacia Guest House
venues.note: A restored 1913 house of just five rooms around a courtyard, warm, personal and among the most charming small stays in Roma.

venues.name: Quintonil
venues.note: Jorge Vallejo and Alejandra Flores' temple to Mexican produce, herbs, heirloom corn and native ingredients at the very peak of world dining.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025, No. 3 (Best in North America)

venues.name: Pujol
venues.note: Enrique Olvera's landmark, the mole madre, aged for years and served in a ring beside a fresh mole, remains one of gastronomy's great dishes.

venues.name: Máximo Bistrot
venues.note: Eduardo 'Lalo' García's bright, produce-driven room, French technique and Mexican soul, cooked from the day's market.

venues.name: Rosetta
venues.note: Elena Reygadas' cooking in a romantic Roma townhouse, Italian roots and Mexican produce from the World's Best Female Chef.

venues.name: Sud 777
venues.note: Edgar Núñez's garden-driven cooking in the leafy south, much of the produce grown in the restaurant's own beds.

venues.name: Em
venues.note: Lucho Martínez's intimate counter, a personal, fire-led tasting menu that was among the guide's most talked-about stars.

venues.name: Esquina Común
venues.note: A young, produce-obsessed kitchen turning Mexican ingredients into a precise, evolving tasting menu, a quiet critical favourite.

venues.name: Expendio de Maíz
venues.note: A tiny, counter-only corn kitchen with no fixed menu, cooking is dictated by what the market gives, heirloom masa at its centre.

venues.name: Masala y Maíz
venues.note: Norma Listman and Saqib Keval's dialogue between Mexican, Indian and East African kitchens, one of the city's most original tables.

venues.name: Taquería El Califa de León
venues.note: A stand-up taquería the size of a garage, awarded a Michelin star for a single thing done to perfection, the gaonera taco.
credentials: MICHELIN ★ (2025), the first taquería in the world to earn a star

venues.name: Contramar
venues.note: Gabriela Cámara's sunlit seafood institution, the tuna tostada and the split-colour pescado a la talla are city rituals.

venues.name: Vigneron
venues.note: A wine-led French bistro from a serious sommelier team, precise cooking built around an exceptional cellar.

venues.name: Comedor Jacinta
venues.note: Chef Edgar Núñez's warm ode to Mexican home cooking, grandmother's recipes plated with real care, in a bright Polanco room.

venues.name: Galanga Thai House
venues.note: Vivid, genuinely spicy Thai cooking in a small Roma house, a Bib favourite and a welcome change of register.

venues.name: Molino El Pujol
venues.note: Enrique Olvera's neighbourhood mill and kitchen, heirloom corn ground on site, turned into tortillas, tamales and simple, brilliant plates.

venues.name: Comal Oculto
venues.note: A produce-led, comal-driven kitchen turning market vegetables and heirloom corn into a considered, good-value menu.

venues.name: Taquería Los Cocuyos
venues.note: A round-the-clock street stand in the old centre, slow-cooked meats and the suadero taco that locals swear by.

venues.name: El Vilsito
venues.note: A mechanic's garage by day, a legendary al pastor taquería by night, one of the city's benchmark trompos.

venues.name: Filigrana
venues.note: A refined-yet-relaxed kitchen doing modern Mexican cooking with real polish, at genuine value.

venues.name: The Zócalo (Plaza de la Constitución)
venues.note: One of the largest city squares on earth, laid over the sacred heart of Aztec Tenochtitlán, where a vast national flag is raised and lowered by the army each day. A private guide reads the layered history for the whole family before the crowds and the altitude tell on anyone.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Metropolitan Cathedral (Catedral Metropolitana)
venues.note: The largest and oldest cathedral in Latin America, a 250-year Spanish Baroque masterpiece slowly sinking into the old lakebed, you feel the floor tilt as you walk toward the altar. Cool, quiet and shaded, a gentle first stop for elders on a busy day.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Templo Mayor & Museum
venues.note: The excavated main temple of Tenochtitlán, unearthed beside the cathedral, with a superb museum holding the great stone disc of the goddess Coyolxauhqui. A guide brings the ruins alive for children who might otherwise see only rubble.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Palacio Nacional & Diego Rivera Murals
venues.note: Rivera's monumental staircase murals, sixteen years of work sweeping across all of Mexican history, line a working seat of government on the Zócalo's east side. Entry is free with photo ID; a guide is essential to decode the crowded, political panels.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
venues.note: A dazzling white-marble Art Nouveau and Art Deco palace crowned with a Tiffany glass stage curtain, holding murals by Rivera, Siqueiros and Orozco. The evening Ballet Folklórico de México here, pre- and post-Hispanic dance staged since 1952, is a beautiful, wordless family night.

venues.name: Ballet Folklórico de México
venues.note: Amalia Hernández's legendary company performs its riot of regional Mexican dance under the Tiffany curtain of Bellas Artes twice weekly. No language needed, so grandparents and children share the same spectacle; private box seats can be arranged.

venues.name: Torre Latinoamericana Observation Deck
venues.note: The 1956 skyscraper that survived every great earthquake gives a 44th-floor panorama of the endless valley city, best at dusk with a drink in the sky-lounge below. A quick, easy way to grasp the sheer scale before diving into the streets.

venues.name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
venues.note: The world's greatest museum of Mesoamerican civilisation, 22 vast halls holding the Aztec Sun Stone, colossal Olmec heads and Maya treasures under a soaring stone-and-water canopy. Too big to see whole; a private guide curates a two-hour path so no one tires.

venues.name: Chapultepec Castle (Museo Nacional de Historia)
venues.note: The only true royal castle in the Americas, crowning the forested hill where Emperor Maximilian once lived, now a history museum with hilltop gardens and city views. A gentle uphill or short shuttle; the terraces reward the climb.

venues.name: Museo Tamayo
venues.note: Rufino Tamayo's own gift to the city, a striking concrete pavilion in Chapultepec woods showing international and Mexican contemporary art. Calm, uncrowded and air-conditioned, a refined counterpoint to the grand anthropology halls next door.

venues.name: Museo de Arte Moderno (MAM)
venues.note: Home to icons of 20th-century Mexican art, including Frida Kahlo's famous 'The Two Fridas' and works by Rivera, Siqueiros and Remedios Varo. A compact, digestible collection set in a sculpture garden, easy to pair with the surrounding park.

venues.name: Bosque de Chapultepec
venues.note: One of the largest urban parks in the Western Hemisphere, twice the size of Central Park, its lakes, forests and museums lending the whole family room to breathe at altitude. A private guide and driver make its scattered sights effortless in a day.

venues.name: Museo Frida Kahlo (Casa Azul)
venues.note: The cobalt-blue house where Frida was born, lived with Diego and died, her studio, wheelchair, corsets and garden left as they were, deeply moving even to those who know little of her art. Timed tickets sell out; a concierge secures a quiet slot in advance.

venues.name: Museo Casa de León Trotsky
venues.note: The fortified house where the exiled revolutionary lived under Frida and Diego's protection and was assassinated in 1940, his study frozen at the moment of the ice-axe blow. A short walk from Casa Azul; a compelling, sombre stop for older travellers with a taste for history.

venues.name: Museo Diego Rivera Anahuacalli
venues.note: Rivera's black-volcanic-stone 'temple of the arts', a pyramid-like fortress he built to house his immense collection of pre-Columbian pieces, set in an ecological reserve. Included with the Casa Azul ticket and blessedly serene, a hidden gem few tourists reach.

venues.name: Coyoacán Historic Centre & Market
venues.note: Cobbled colonial squares, twin plazas, fountains and a lively covered market of textiles, crafts and tostadas make this the city's most enchanting village-within-a-city. Leafy and walkable, it suits a slow multi-generational afternoon with plenty of shaded benches.

venues.name: Bazar Sábado & San Ángel
venues.note: Every Saturday this cobbled colonial quarter fills with a genteel art-and-artisan bazaar around Plaza San Jacinto, from fine silver to painting. Compact and refined shopping with courtyard restaurants, a graceful morning for shoppers of all ages.

venues.name: Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo
venues.note: The pair of bold functionalist studio-houses, one pink, one blue, linked by a rooftop bridge, designed by Juan O'Gorman for the artists, a landmark of Mexican modernism. Quiet and architectural, a fine companion to a San Ángel stroll.

venues.name: Museo Soumaya
venues.note: Carlos Slim's free museum, a shimmering twist of 16,000 mirrored steel tiles, holds the largest Rodin collection outside France alongside old masters and Mexican art. Architecturally jaw-dropping and easily woven into a Polanco shopping day.

venues.name: Museo Jumex
venues.note: David Chipperfield's crisp travertine gallery next to the Soumaya houses Latin America's finest private contemporary-art collection. A cool, curated hour for serious collectors, with a good café, a refined pause between boutiques.

venues.name: Avenida Presidente Masaryk Luxury Shopping
venues.note: Mexico's most expensive avenue, a leafy boulevard of Louis Vuitton, Hermès, Cartier, Bulgari and Tiffany showrooms alongside acclaimed restaurants. Discreet, tree-lined and easy for a driver to shadow, the natural base for luxury travellers.

venues.name: Casa Luis Barragán (Casa Estudio)
venues.note: The Pritzker laureate's own house and studio, a serene interplay of light, colour and volume that is the touchstone of modern Mexican architecture. Strictly small guided groups by reservation only, a quiet, unmissable pilgrimage for design lovers.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Luis Barragán House and Studio

venues.name: Xochimilco Trajineras
venues.note: The last living remnant of the Aztec lake, where flower-painted trajinera barges glide through canals and floating chinampa gardens, mariachis drifting alongside. A private boat with catered food and mezcal turns it into a joyful, safe family afternoon.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Teotihuacán Pyramids (Day Trip)
venues.note: An hour from the city rise the vast Pyramids of the Sun and Moon along the Avenue of the Dead, a metropolis older and grander than the Aztecs who revered it. Go early with a private guide and driver, or float above it all at dawn in a hot-air balloon.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan

venues.name: Arena México, Lucha Libre
venues.note: The 'Cathedral of Lucha Libre', where masked luchadores fly from the ropes to roaring, family-friendly crowds, pure, joyful Mexican theatre. A curated evening with ringside seats and a guide (skip the rougher streets outside) is a memory kids never forget.

venues.name: Mercado de San Juan
venues.note: The gourmet market of the city, famed for exotic ingredients, fine cheeses, jamón and stalls where chefs shop, a feast for food-curious travellers. A guide can steer vegetarians to the produce, cheese and prepared-food counters that suit.

venues.name: Mercado de Artesanías La Ciudadela
venues.note: The city's best one-stop craft market, aisles of Talavera pottery, Oaxacan textiles, silver, alebrijes and Day-of-the-Dead art under one roof. Fixed and calm enough for relaxed, unhurried gift-buying with the family.

venues.name: Parque México & Parque España
venues.note: Two lush Art Deco parks at the heart of leafy Condesa, ringed by 1920s architecture, dog-walkers and pavement cafés. A gentle, green stroll that lets multi-gen groups slow down and simply feel the city's most liveable neighbourhood.

venues.name: Roma Norte Galleries & Dining
venues.note: Belle Époque mansions now hold design shops, art galleries and some of the city's finest restaurants along tree-lined Álvaro Obregón. Walkable, stylish and full of tasting menus that thoughtfully accommodate vegetarians on request.

venues.name: Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL)
venues.note: A palatial Beaux-Arts building housing four centuries of Mexican painting and sculpture, from colonial altarpieces to the great landscapes of José María Velasco. Grand, uncrowded and beautifully told by a private guide.

venues.name: Museo del Templo de la Enseñanza & Calle Madero Walk
venues.note: The pedestrian Madero street links Bellas Artes to the Zócalo past the tiled Casa de los Azulejos and ornate churches, the finest colonial promenade in the city. Flat, car-free and easy for elders, threading the Centro's greatest hits in one walk.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Museo del Objeto del Objeto (MODO)
venues.note: A witty, one-of-a-kind design museum of everyday Mexican objects and advertising, set in an Art Nouveau townhouse. Small, playful and unexpected, a light, charming stop that amuses children and grown-ups alike.

venues.name: Biblioteca Vasconcelos
venues.note: A soaring 'megalibrary' of suspended glass floors and a whale skeleton hovering in the void, one of the world's most photographed modern libraries. A quick, awe-inducing detour that thrills teenagers and architecture buffs.

venues.name: Monumento a la Revolución & Mirador
venues.note: A colossal Art Deco arch, tomb of revolutionary heroes, with a glass lift rising to a rooftop viewing deck above Reforma. Fast and striking, with a fine panorama and a plaza that dances with fountains at night.

venues.name: Ángel de la Independencia & Paseo de la Reforma
venues.note: The golden Angel of Independence presides over Mexico's grand Haussmann-style boulevard, lined with monuments, hotels and Sunday cyclists. A driver's slow cruise here orients the family to the modern city's spine.

venues.name: Basílica de Santa María de Guadalupe
venues.note: Mexico's most sacred shrine, where the miraculous image of the Virgin of Guadalupe draws millions, its modern circular basilica beside the old sinking one. A moving, deeply human place; a guide navigates the vast pilgrim crowds respectfully.

venues.name: Jardín Centenario & Coyoacán Churches
venues.note: The garden square framed by the 16th-century San Juan Bautista church and the coyote fountain is the soul of old Coyoacán, alive with musicians and ice-cream sellers. Shaded, sociable and endlessly photogenic for an easy family hour.

venues.name: Mercado Roma
venues.note: A multi-storey gourmet food hall with rooftop terrace gathering the city's best artisan producers, taquerías and mezcal bars under one stylish roof. Curated and comfortable, with clearly labelled options for vegetarian members of the party.

venues.name: Cineteca Nacional & Mezcal Tasting
venues.note: Mexico's cinematheque is a sleek cultural campus of open-air screens and cafés, and the surrounding south is dotted with refined mezcalerías. A private tasting flight, smoky espadín to rare tobalá, reveals Mexico's soul in a glass, guided and unhurried.

venues.name: Puebla (Day Trip)
venues.note: Two hours east, a UNESCO colonial jewel of Talavera-tiled facades, gilded churches and mole poblano beneath the Popocatépetl volcano. A private car makes it a gracious full day of architecture, cuisine and artisan ceramics.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Puebla

venues.name: Tepoztlán (Day Trip)
venues.note: A magical mountain 'Pueblo Mágico' an hour south, crowned by the cliff-top Tepozteco pyramid, ringed by mystic peaks, market stalls and a warmer climate. A relaxed day for wellness and nature, with the pyramid hike optional for the fitter.

venues.name: Museo Kaluz
venues.note: A refined newer museum in a restored colonial hospice by the Alameda, showing Mexican art across five centuries, with a rooftop terrace over Bellas Artes. Elegant, calm and rarely crowded, a connoisseur's stop with a fine view.

venues.name: Museo Nacional de las Culturas del Mundo & Moneda Street
venues.note: Behind the cathedral, this world-cultures museum sits on a beautiful colonial street of Rivera murals in the old Mint. A quiet, free-flowing detour a step off the Zócalo's bustle.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Jardín Botánico & Chapultepec Zoo
venues.note: Within the great park, a serene botanical garden and a free zoo home to giant pandas make a gentle, green interlude. Ideal for younger children in the multi-gen group when the museums have run long.

venues.name: Templo de San Francisco & Casa de los Azulejos
venues.note: On Madero, a graceful old Franciscan church faces the House of Tiles, a blue-and-white Talavera-clad palace now a landmark café. A quick, atmospheric pairing of church and courtyard in the heart of the walk.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco

venues.name: Mercado de Coyoacán Antojitos
venues.note: The covered market's food aisles serve legendary tostadas, quesadillas and aguas frescas in a festive, colourful setting. A guide can point vegetarians to the many meat-free antojitos so no one misses out on the fun.

venues.name: Six Flags & Bosque de Tlalpan (Southern Green Escape)
venues.note: For families with children, the forested Bosque de Tlalpan offers easy trails and clean mountain air on the city's southern edge, a calm antidote to museum days. Peaceful, safe and green, the local families' weekend refuge.

venues.name: Handshake Speakeasy
venues.note: Eric van Beek's precision cocktail temple, now in grander premises in Juárez, technique-driven, theatrical drinks at the very top of the craft.
credentials: North America's 50 Best Bars 2025, No. 1 (Best Bar in North America)

venues.name: Licorería Limantour
venues.note: The bar that lit the fuse of Mexico City's cocktail renaissance, polished, inventive drinks and a benchmark for the whole scene.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars 2025, No. 52 (extended list)

venues.name: Baltra Bar
venues.note: A tiny, Galápagos-themed Condesa bar of quiet obsession, one of the city's most respected rooms for the seriously made classic.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars 2025, No. 78 (extended list)

venues.name: Rayo
venues.note: An agave-devoted bar built around the myth of Mayahuel, mezcal, tequila and pulque woven into story-driven, thoughtful cocktails.

venues.name: Hanky Panky
venues.note: A hidden speakeasy behind an unmarked door, one of the city's original cocktail dens, still buzzing late into the night.

venues.name: Kaito del Valle
venues.note: A Japanese-leaning cocktail bar of real precision, omakase-style drinks and a hushed, considered room away from the tourist trail.

venues.name: Bijou Drinkery Room
venues.note: A small, jewel-like bar with a sharp, spirit-forward list, a critics' favourite that punches far above its size.

venues.name: Ticuchi
venues.note: Enrique Olvera's agave bar beside Pujol, a dark, atmospheric room devoted to mezcal and its cousins, with cooking to match.
credentials: North America's 50 Best Bars 2025, No. 82 (extended list)

venues.name: Cityzen, Sofitel Mexico City Reforma
venues.note: The Sofitel's 38th-floor rooftop bar, the definitive high-altitude drink over Reforma and the Angel of Independence.
credentials: Atop a MICHELIN One-Key hotel, the city's premier skyline rooftop
